steps: Unpack & inspect

Check the stove and parts (shipped in the ash pan) for transit damage. The catalyst packing burns off in the first fire. Door and bypass handles ship inside the stove: fit them after final positioning.

Report damaged or missing parts to your authorized Hearthstone dealer right away. The label hangs on a cable under the stove: don't damage it when lifting. After final positioning, store it in the holding clip on the bottom shield.

Pack listStove, owner's manual, wood handles, screws and washers
Choose the location
Freestanding room heater only, never in a factory-built fireplace. Prefer a main living area to a basement, and check clearances to walls, floor, ceiling and chimney chase before connecting.
Floor protection
Noncombustible protection under the stove, extending 16" US / 18" Canada at the side door and front, 5" at the other side and 2" at the rear, measured from the body. No insulated pad needed.
Clearances

Take wall clearances from the Figure 3 table for the connector used (single-wall, single-wall with heat shield, double-wall with heat shield). Check alcove minimums and the Figure 5 trim and mantel drawing.
Outside air (if used)
Kit 90-53220 to a min. 3" duct, terminated no higher than the stove's intake, screened and hooded. Required in mobile homes; in Canada add a 100%-closing damper and fasten the stove to the floor.
Top-to-rear flue conversion (if used)
To vent out the rear, swap the top flue collar and the rear flue plate using a 7/16" wrench.

1. Remove the four bolts holding the top flue collar to the top casting; don't drop bolts or washers into the stove. Set the collar aside.
  2. Reach through the top opening and remove the top two bolts and washers holding the rear flue plate.
  3. Loosen the bottom two bolts until the plate is free and remove it. Leave the bottom two bolts in place.
  4. Hold the bottom two bolts and position the flue collar in the rear exit position. Hand-tighten the bottom two bolts slightly.
  5. Insert the top two bolts with washers into the top two threaded holes of the flue plate, then fully tighten all four.
  6. Place the flue plate on the top opening, align the holes, and install and tighten the bolts and washers.
Chimney connector
6" 24 or 25 MSG blued steel, crimped ends toward the stove, three #10 x 1/2" sheet metal screws at every joint. Keep it short and straight; horizontal runs rise at least 1/4" per foot.

No aluminum or galvanized pipe. The connector can't pass through a floor, ceiling, attic, roof space, closet or similar concealed space. Through a combustible wall, use a thimble or pass-through per NFPA 211 or CAN/CSA-B365 (four constructions, A to D, on p. 12). Never connect to a flue used by another appliance or to an air distribution duct. Telescoping pipe, slip connectors or a clean-out tee ease inspection.
Chimney & draft
Listed Type HT (2100° F) chimney per UL 103 or ULC S629, or a code-approved lined masonry chimney; 6" flue. Check the draft at installation: 0.06" to 0.1" WC, with a stovepipe damper above 0.1".

Masonry: brick or block at least 4" thick, or rubble or stone, always lined. Tile liner with at least 5/8" wall, refractory mortar and 1" air space, or a UL listed 6" stainless liner, insulated or wrapped. Have the chimney examined and repaired first; the cleanout door must seal. Chimney heights are on p. 17.
Mobile home installs
Per 24 CFR Part 3280 (HUD): outside air kit, stove fastened to the floor with the shipping clips, listed mobile home chimney and connector kit with spark arrester. Never in a sleeping room.

• Kit (UL103 or ULC-S629): stainless spark arrester cap, storm collar, adjustable vented flashing 0/12 – 6/12, two 24" chimney pipes, 24" support box with starter section and trim.
  • Chimney attached directly to the stove; at least 3 feet above the roof it passes through, with its top at least 2 feet above any part of the home within 10 feet.
  • Roof terminations removable without special tools at or below 13-1/2 feet above ground. Remove the chimney when transporting the home.
  • Wall exits 7 feet or less above ground need a guard up to 7 feet.
  • Maintain the structural integrity of walls, floor, ceiling and roof.

panels.title: Stove smokes
items: Operating technique → fully open the primary air one minute before opening doors, and open the bypass first
Cold chimney or reverse draft → preheat the chimney; briefly open a window
Blocked chimney → check chimney and stovepipe for blockage or creosote
Chimney oversized, undersized or too short → reline, add a draft inducer or replace, or lengthen
Air leaking into the chimney → seal connections and openings; check clean-out doors
Bypass not closed or catalyst not working → close it once active; inspect, brush or replace the catalyst
Wet fuel or another appliance on the flue → seasoned, dry cordwood; disconnect other appliances

panels.title: Back-puffing or gas explosions
items: Operating technique → air fully open one minute before opening the door and for a few minutes after reloading; bypass open first
Extra low burn rate → burn at a higher rate
Chimney down-draft → install a chimney cap
Excessive ash build-up → empty the ash pan more often; avoid poor or green wood

panels.title: Uncontrolled or short burn
items: Unsealed or open door, leaking glass gasket → close the door tightly; replace gaskets
Excessive draft → check the install, operate at low burn; over 0.1 wc needs stovepipe damper(s)
Extra long chimney → shorten it or add stovepipe damper(s)
Oversized chimney → reline to the proper diameter
High winds or hilltop location → install a chimney cap

panels.title: Insufficient heat
items: Check first: a 400° F stovepipe, measured no more than 12 inches above the flue collar, means the stove is making enough heat
Poor, low-Btu or green wood → air-dried wood, dried at least one year
Low burn rate → operate at a higher burn rate
Cold exterior chimney or leaky venting → reline or insulate; check the installation
Heat loss from the house → insulate, upgrade or caulk windows, seal openings

light.title: Lighting an everyday fire
light.html:
Use these steps once the stove is broken in.

  1. Open the bypass handle, then open the front door.
  2. Put five or six double sheets of tightly twisted newspaper in the center of the firebox. Stand about 10 pieces of kindling, 1/2" in diameter and 10" to 16" long, over it like a tee-pee.
  3. Slide the primary air control fully to the left. That's fully open.
  4. Light the paper. Leave the door slightly open for a moment, until the kindling catches and the draft starts to pull. Then close the door.
  5. Once the kindling is burning, add logs, small ones first. Keep them toward the center, away from the glass.
  6. When the fire is burning well and the catalyst probe reads Active, close the bypass.
  7. Let it run on high for about 20 minutes so the catalyst stays active. Then set the burn rate with the air control.

Reloading

Always open the bypass before you open the door. Open the door a crack, pause, then open it fully. Load onto a bed of hot, red coals, leaving a small valley in the coals behind the lower primary air opening. Run it at a medium to high rate until the catalyst reaches about 600 °F, then close the bypass.

Note: p. 24 says to run the stove at a medium to high firing rate for about 10 minutes after reloading; p. 31 says to burn it with the primary air fully open for 15 to 20 minutes after reloading, to minimize creosote buildup.

breakin.title: Breaking in a new stove
breakin.html:
Soapstone has to be seasoned. Its natural moisture must be driven out slowly, and the furnace cement must cure slowly. Firing a new stove too hard can crack the soapstone or damage other parts.

  1. Open the bypass handle. Put five or six double sheets of tightly twisted newspaper in the center of the firebox, with about ten pieces of kindling crisscrossed on top.
  2. Pull the primary air control fully to the left.
  3. Light the paper. Leave the door slightly open for a moment until the kindling catches, then close it.
  4. Keep a steady, low fire. The stove should feel warm, not hot. Steam, boiling moisture or hissing means the soapstone is too hot. Add a few small chunks of wood at most.
  5. Once it's warm, push the air control fully in toward the stove and let the fire die out.
  6. Let the stove cool to room temperature.

Build your first fire, and the first fire of every season, this way.

Some smoke and smell is normal. Paints and oils off-gas during the first fires. Open a few windows. It usually fades after 10 to 20 minutes and ends once the stove is cured.

After break-in, check the stovepipe and chimney and clean them if needed: cool fires can build creosote quickly. In time the soapstone may change color and show small surface fractures, which don't affect how it works. A panel that breaks completely must be replaced.

bypass.title: The bypass and the catalyst probe
bypass.html:
Smoke can go around the catalyst or through it. The bypass handle decides which.

Handle toward the frontBypass open: smoke goes around the catalyst
Handle toward the rearBypass closed: smoke goes through the catalyst
  • Open it when you start a fire, until the catalyst heats up, and every time you open the front door to load.
  • Close it once the catalyst is up to temperature, and keep it closed while the stove burns in the active range.

Reading the probe

The probe shows the temperature just past the catalyst. It should sit 3/8" from the body of the stove.

InactiveKeep the bypass open until the stove heats up
ActiveClose the bypass
Too HotKeep the door closed, fully close the air control, and let it cool back to Active

Once it's active, the burning smoke keeps the catalyst hot as long as there's fuel in the stove. The stove typically runs between 800 °F and 1300 °F.

burn.title: Burn rate and over-firing
burn.html:
The primary air control handle sits at the lower left front, just under the ash lip. More air gives a faster, hotter fire; less air gives a slower one.

HighAll the way to the left (fully open)
MediumAnywhere in between; experiment to find your setting
LowAll the way to the right (minimum opening)
  • The air control never closes completely. That minimum is set at the factory, and federal rules forbid changing it.
  • For a high burn, fully load the firebox onto hot coals or an actively flaming fire.
  • Long stretches on low can build creosote. If you often burn low, check the venting often.
  • Run it on high once or twice a day for 35 to 45 minutes to heat the stovepipe and chimney.
  • Keep the door closed while it burns. Leave it ajar only briefly while lighting.

Over-firing

Over-firing means running hotter than a normal high burn. Signs include warped parts, short burn times, a roaring sound in the stove or stovepipe, and discolored stovepipe. Causes include too much draft, the wrong fuel, worn gaskets, or burning with a door open.

Never over-fire the stove. It will damage the stove. If you suspect over-firing, stop using the stove and call your dealer immediately. Over-fire damage isn't covered, and any sign of over-firing voids the warranty.

wood.title: Choosing firewood
wood.html:
Burn only natural cordwood. This stove isn't designed for any other fuel.

  • Dry it first. Split, stack and air-dry green wood for a year. Seasoned wood is at or near 20% moisture; a hand-held moisture meter will tell you. Green wood may give less than 2000 Btu per pound; dry wood can give up to 7000 Btu per pound.
  • Stack it right. Keep it off the ground on skids or blocks and cover only the top. Tarps over the sides trap moisture.
  • Hardwood or softwood. Softwoods burn hotter and faster; hardwoods burn longer and leave better coals. The manual's heat-value chart puts hickory, black locust and white oak in its top group, and aspen, white pine, basswood and cottonwood in its lowest.
  • Don't store firewood inside the stove's required clearances, and never load ice-covered wood into a burning stove.
Never burn coal, charcoal, pellets, artificial or wax logs, garbage or trash, lawn clippings, materials containing rubber (including tires), materials containing plastic, waste petroleum products, paints or paint thinners, solvents, flammable fluids, asphalt products, materials containing asbestos, construction or demolition debris, railroad ties, manure or animal remains, paper products (including colored or glossy paper), cardboard, plywood, particleboard, driftwood (including salt water driftwood) or other previously salt water saturated materials, unseasoned wood, or painted, treated, pressure treated or kiln-dried wood. Burning these materials may release toxic fumes, make the stove ineffective, cause smoke and damage the catalyst. Never use gasoline, kerosene, lighter fluid or other chemicals to start or freshen a fire. Fire starters made of paper, cardboard, sawdust or wax are fine for lighting.

ash.title: Removing and storing ashes
ash.html:
Empty the ashes at the end of every week, sooner if the firebox is full. Let the fire die down or go out first.

  • A thin layer of ash in the firebox is fine. Don't let ash build up at the front door opening: it spills out or packs into the gasket channel and stops the door sealing.
  • Use a fireplace shovel. Push large live coals to the side and take out only the finer ash.
  • With the optional ash pan, open the ash door and slide the ash grate toward the front door to sift ash into the pan, then close the grate. Push the pan in hard before you pull it out. Only run the stove with the pan in and the ash door closed.

Storing them

  • Put ashes straight into a metal container with a tight-fitting lid. Nothing else goes in it, and don't pour water in.
  • Set it on a noncombustible floor or on the ground outside, well away from anything that burns, liquid fuels and vehicles. Never on a combustible surface or vinyl flooring.
  • Keep the lid on until the coals are completely cool. Coals in ash can stay hot for several days.
  • Never use wooden or plastic containers, paper or plastic bags, or a trash can with other trash.

glass.title: Glass and door gasket
glass.html:
The door glass is a tough ceramic rated to 2300° F, but scratches weaken it. Clean it only when the fire is out and the glass is cool.

  1. Inside: dip a damp paper towel in gray ash and rub in circles.
  2. When the deposits are off, finish with window cleaner or a commercial stove-glass cleaner, inside and out.
  3. Wipe it off with a soft cloth or black-and-white newsprint.

Never use a razor blade, steel wool or anything abrasive. Glass that's always dirty means the fire runs too cool or the wood is wet.

Note: p. 31 suggests window cleaner or a commercial stove-glass cleaner for the glass, then says to use only a cleaner made specifically for woodstoves.

If the glass is cracked, chipped or broken, don't use the stove until it's replaced (glass kit 90-58215).

Note: p. 30 says only a qualified service person should replace the glass; p. 32 says the glass kit includes everything needed for the repair and, if you replace the glass yourself, to wear work gloves and safety glasses.

Door gasket

Every other month, with the stove cool, shut the door on a dollar bill. If it pulls out with no resistance, adjust the latch or replace the gasket. Replace it every two to three seasons, or when it's worn or loose, with a Hearthstone gasket kit (90-58230).

catalyst.title: Caring for the catalyst
catalyst.html:
The catalyst burns up smoke the firebox missed. One that stops working costs you heat and adds creosote and emissions. Never run the stove with the catalysts removed.

Check it

  • Look at the catalyst at least three times each heating season.
  • A working catalyst normally stays above 500 °F and often goes past 1,000 °F. If yours doesn't get above 500 °F, see the catalyst troubleshooting chart (p. 34).
  • Smoke test: with the smoke going through the catalyst, go outside and look at the chimney. Then open the bypass and look again. You should see much more smoke in bypass mode.

Brush it (stove and ashes fully cool)

  1. Pull the cotter pin and lift the baffle retainer up and away.
  2. Gently ease the front baffle forward, over the front tube and out. Don't force it.
  3. Clear ash and soot off the face of the catalyst with a soft-bristled brush or small vacuum nozzle.
  4. Look for warping, corrosion or plugged openings. If you find any, the catalyst blocks need to come out for a closer look (p. 28).
  5. Put the baffle and retainer back in reverse order.

chimney.title: Creosote and chimney fires
chimney.html:
Creosote is a tar that condenses in the chimney when wood burns slowly and cool. If it ignites, it burns extremely hot and can damage the chimney or even destroy the house.

  • At first, check for creosote daily until you learn how fast it builds. You may need to clean weekly in mild weather; monthly may be enough in the coldest months.
  • Inspect the chimney connector and chimney at least every two months in the heating season. Remove creosote thicker than 1/4".
  • Hotter fires leave less creosote. Burn with the air fully open for 35 to 45 minutes daily.
  • Before each heating season, have the whole system professionally inspected, cleaned and repaired. A certified chimney sweep is recommended.

If you have a stovepipe or chimney fire

  1. If it's too threatening, leave and call the fire department right away.
  2. Otherwise, close the primary air control.
  3. Close the stovepipe damper, if you have one.
  4. Close the bypass.
  5. Keep the front door closed.
Never throw water on the stove, stovepipe or chimney: the instant steam can seriously hurt you. Once the fire is out, keep the air and bypass closed and let the stove die out. Have everything inspected, and fix any damage, before using it again.

warranty.title: Warranty at a glance
warranty.html:
Hearthstone covers defects in material or workmanship for the original retail purchaser only. It isn't transferable, and the stove must be installed by an authorized Hearthstone dealer or their designated representative. Coverage starts on your original invoice date. "Limited Lifetime" means 10 years.

Which parts get Limited Lifetime, 5-, 3-, 2- or 1-year coverage is shown as a check-mark grid on p. 38.

Warranty laborFirst year, if a dealer installed it
Parts shippingFirst 90 days
Appliance shippingFirst year, split 50/50

The catalyst

Its maker, Applied Ceramics, replaces it at no charge if it stops working within two (2) years. After that it's prorated: $130.00 in year 3, rising to $160.00 in year 6, then current retail.

Note: p. 37 gives the catalyst's no-charge replacement period as two (2) years, then says one replacement catalyst is given for each defective catalyst returned "during the three year period."

Not covered, for example

  • Over-firing, wrong fuels, or ignoring the manual or codes
  • Wear parts: paint, gaskets, baffles, refractory, ash grates, glass
  • Hairline stone cracks, expansion noise, odors

Claims go through your dealer. Registering at hearthstonestoves.com isn't required for coverage.

specEpa.html:
Particulate emissions1.1 g/hr
Maker's website: EPA Certified 1.1 g/hr in its spec table; its page copy says "At only 0.54 g/hr of particulate emissions, the Heritage is our cleanest burning stove thanks to the TruHybrid system."
StandardEPA 2020, crib wood (Method 28R)
Heat output (test)12,889 to 29,191 Btu/hr
Maker's website: BTU Up to 60,000.
Efficiency77.3% (HHV), weighted average
Maker's website: Efficiency 77% HHV.
CO, categories 1 / 2 / 3 / 40.11 / 0.25 / 0.10 / 4.12 g/min

Output measured with Douglas Fir test wood. Efficiency is weighted across the 4 burn-rate categories (EPA Method 28R and CSA B415-10). The minimum low burn rate is set by the manufacturer and must not be altered.

The manual prints the emission rate as 1.1 gr/hr on p. 2; p. 7 gives 1.1 g/hr.

specFlue.title: Flue and chimney
specFlue.html:
Connector6" (152 mm), 24 or 25 MSG blued steel
Prefab chimneyType HT (2100° F), UL 103 or ULC S629
Flue, new installs6" (152 mm) inside diameter
Existing flue8" with a reducer

Chimney size: not less than the flue collar, and not more than three times its cross-sectional area. An oversized flue adds creosote. No aluminum or galvanized connector. Never connect to a flue serving another appliance or to any air distribution duct. Liner: UL 1777 or ULC S635.

Have a masonry chimney examined by a professional and repaired before installing; the cleanout door must close completely and seal tight. Buy prefab chimney accessories from the chimney's manufacturer.

Some LVP and LVT flooring begins to warp at 110° Fahrenheit. Check the flooring manufacturer's limits; extra shielding may be needed.

Keep furniture, drapes and other combustibles at least 36" from the stove.

review.notes: Wall clearances (Fig. 3 table, p. 10) and connector clearances (Fig. 4, p. 11) are keyed to lettered dimensions defined only in the drawings, so the lettered values were not transcribed; the guide links p. 10. The catalog clearances_note (side 16", rear 16"/6", corner 8") matches the numbers in columns A, B and G of the p. 10 table, but the letter meanings can't be confirmed from text, so it is not listed as a mismatch. Drawings only: trim and mantel clearances (Fig. 5, p. 13), chimney height (Fig. 8, p. 17), typical chimney (Fig. 9, p. 18), lock-down detail (Fig. 10, p. 19), safety label (p. 36). The stove-components warranty (p. 38) is a Wood/Gas/Pellet check-mark grid; rows with a single mark are ambiguous, so coverage periods per part were not transcribed and the drawer points to p. 38. p. 7 prints maximum heat output as '29.191 BTUs per hour'; p. 2 gives 12,889 to 29,191 Btu/hr. Treated as a punctuation slip; the guide uses 29,191. Break-in kindling is '10" to 16" (254 mm to 457 mm)' while everyday kindling is '10" to 16" (254 mm to 406 mm)' (both p. 24); the guide uses inches only. Chimney-fire steps (p. 6) say 'perform the next three steps' but list four (air, damper, bypass, door); all four are shown. Stale cross-references in the manual: p. 5 chimney cleaning 'see page 28' (creosote is p. 31) and ash disposal 'see page 23' (p. 26); p. 13 lock-down 'page 17' (p. 19); p. 14 spark arrester 'page 18' (p. 19); p. 19 outside air 'page 12' (p. 13); p. 28 catalyst warranty 'page 35' (p. 37); p. 26 'section 3.3.5'; p. 17 'Figure 9' for chimney height (Fig. 8). All pagerefs use the physical pages where the topics appear. p. 8 says parts ship in the ash pan, yet the ash pan is listed as optional (90-54240) on pp. 20 and 35. p. 29 prints the rear-baffle procedure three times. p. 22 says unauthorized fuel such as coal could produce high levels of 'carbon dioxide'; p. 19 says burning other fuels could generate dangerous carbon monoxide. Neither is quoted. Top-to-rear conversion step 5 (p. 14) says 'threaded holes of flue plate' while the collar is being fitted at the rear; kept as worded, check against the figure. The manual describes the primary air control both as left (open) / right (closed) and as pull toward you / push in toward the stove; these agree. btu_output_epa 29191 matches p. 2, so it is not listed as a mismatch. Oct 12: the website's Efficiency 77% HHV (the manual's 77.3% rounded) and the 0.54 g/hr emissions figure in its page copy are now listed in catalog_mismatches and noted in the specEpa drawer.
